947: Eq. (F4) is a simple substitutional liquid model that splits the liquid free energy of a binary A–B system into the pure-element reference, ideal mixing and the deviation from ideal mixing. The pressure is held constant and the pressure dependence is omitted in the equation.
950: Atomic fraction of B in the liquid. The atomic fraction of A is 1−x.
952: Gibbs free energy per atom of pure liquid A and pure liquid B at the same temperature and pressure. These are temperature-dependent pure-element functions.
954: Here the symbol for the pure-element reference state. It does not mean 0 K.
955: Excess Gibbs free energy of the liquid phase. It represents the deviation from the ideal solution.
956: Pure-element terms: the first two terms are the reference formed by the free energies of pure liquid A and pure liquid B, each weighted by its atomic fraction.
957: Ideal-mixing term: the term containing logarithms is the free-energy contribution of the ideal configurational entropy multiplied by −T. It is zero at the pure-element end points and negative at mixed compositions at positive temperature.
958: Excess term: represents the non-ideality due to, for example, interactions between unlike atoms. It can contain not only enthalpy but also non-ideal entropy contributions. It is zero for an ideal solution.
959: Units: in eq. (F4) all free-energy terms are expressed in eV/atom and the Boltzmann constant is used in eV/K. When writing in J/mol-atoms, the Boltzmann constant is replaced by the gas constant R, and the pure-element and excess terms are all converted to the same molar units.
960: A TDB containing the interaction terms and pure-element functions of the target system is used. The absolute energies of the MLIP are not added directly to the TDB but converted to a common elemental reference state. Since the total free energy of eq. (F4) already contains the ideal-mixing term, the configurational entropy is not added again.
961: The quantum harmonic solid has zero-point vibrations, while ordinary classical MD liquids do not. When combining the two, the consistency of the nuclear quantum effects is checked, and one chooses and records either unification to the classical limit, a quantum correction, or an assessment of the effect of omitting it. Ordinary phonons of a liquid snapshot are not used as the absolute free energy of the liquid.
962: 5 supplement. The route using an existing CALPHAD database
963: An existing database can be used not only for the liquid but also for the free-energy models of pure elements, solid solutions, ordered phases and line phases. A CALPHAD database (TDB is one example of an exchange format) gives the temperature- and composition-dependent model and parameters for each phase, and equilibrium-calculation software uses them to determine the phase boundaries.
966: Compute all phases from an existing database
967: Compute the equilibrium phase diagram from a database that contains the target element system and phases. If the required models are all present, no new phonon or MD calculations for the individual phases are needed to obtain the phase diagram.
968: Adopt some phases from an existing database
969: For example, take the liquid and the terminal solid solutions from the database and evaluate compounds not included with the MLIP. Separate the adopted phases and contributions, and make the reference states of all phases consistent.
970: Supplement and re-assess with MLIP calculations
971: Compute the free energies of the missing composition and temperature ranges or phases, and re-assess the parameters together with the existing experimental and thermodynamic data. Check the boundaries with independent validation data.
973: Compare the MLIP-derived phase diagram with the phase boundaries, solubility ranges and melting points of the existing database. Do not immediately conclude that a difference is an error of the MLIP; check the approximations and range of validity on both sides.
974: Stage 05 in Fig. 1: what "putting on the same reference" means
975: This is the stage that makes the free energies of the phases directly comparable with each other. For example, if the MLIP calculation of the solid returns energies in eV/atom and the CALPHAD model of the liquid returns free energies in J/mol based on a given pure-element reference, those numbers cannot be compared directly.
979: Unify all phases to eV/atom or J/mol-atoms etc. Distinguish quantities per cell, per formula unit and per site.
981: Convert all phases to free energies based on the same pure-element reference.
983: Compare Gibbs free energies at the same temperature and pressure.
985: Check for missing and double-counted configurational, vibrational, electronic etc. contributions. Also make the nuclear quantum effects of the quantum solid and the classical MD liquid consistent.
986: Subtracting the same composition-weighted sum of elemental references from all phases, as in eq. (G1), does not change the phase equilibria. This is because a common function linear in composition is subtracted at fixed temperature and pressure. It is not an operation that sets the minimum of each phase to zero separately. Choosing a different zero point per phase changes the free-energy differences between phases, and hence the common tangents and phase boundaries.
987: When combining results from different MLIPs, DFT and existing databases, a formal application of eq. (G1) is not necessarily sufficient. The difference in references is checked with common calculations such as the pure elements, and the necessary corrections are determined. Physical differences in prediction between models cannot be removed by a zero-point conversion alone.

However, aligning only the zero point of the MLIP atomic energies does not make the temperature dependence agree with an experiment-based TDB. The reference, including the differences between phases of the pure elements, the heat capacity, zero-point vibrations and quantum effects, is checked, and verification is also done at known phase boundaries.
990: Before adoption, check the target element system and phases, the temperature, pressure and composition ranges, the interaction parameters, the sublattice and vacancy models, the units and molar basis, the version, source and terms of use, and the compatibility with the equilibrium-calculation software. To treat the solubility range of an ordered phase, a model that allows composition variation for that phase is needed. A finite solubility range of that phase cannot be obtained from a model that contains it only as a line phase.
